sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Ashtabula County?
sections.html:
The county auditor values property and runs the Board of Revision, while the county treasurer bills and collects the tax. The auditor's office sits in the county courthouse at 25 W Jefferson St in Jefferson, and the main line is 440-576-3783. For anything about a tax bill itself, the payoff amount on a sale, or a delinquent balance, ask the Ashtabula County treasurer.

Ashtabula County is the northeasternmost county in Ohio, with Jefferson as the county seat and the city of Ashtabula as its largest community. The 2020 census counted 97,574 residents and 46,237 housing units, of which 14.9% were vacant. Among occupied homes, 71.0% were owner-occupied.

sections.h2: What is it like to own and sell a house across Ashtabula County?
sections.html:
The county covers 1,368 square miles, and 49% of that is Lake Erie water, which still makes it the largest Ohio county by area. Three cities (Ashtabula, Conneaut and Geneva) sit beside seven villages: Andover, Geneva-on-the-Lake, Jefferson, North Kingsville, Orwell, Roaming Shores and Rock Creek. Interstate 90, US 6, US 20 and State Route 11 are among the numbered highways listed for the county.

  • Lake-effect snow falls often here, because the county lies in the Southeastern Lake Erie Snowbelt, so roofs, gutters and drainage matter to buyers.
  • Nineteen covered bridges and a wine-growing area near the lake draw visitors and shape the rural and seasonal housing mix.
  • The county is part of the Cleveland metropolitan statistical area, and the median age was 43.6 in 2020.

A house in a lakeside village and a farmhouse inland can sit in very different taxing districts, so the parcel number on your bill is the starting point for every question below.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my property value in Ashtabula County?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the Ashtabula County Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31 of the tax year. Ohio's statute, ORC 5715.19(A)(1), sets the deadline as March 31 of the following tax year or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later, and the county's own instructions use the January 1 to March 31 window. A mailed complaint counts on the postmark date, and a private meter postmark does not.

The Board adjusts values, not tax dollars. The owner carries the burden of proof, so bring documents.

  • The closing statement and purchase contract if you bought recently.
  • An independent appraisal.
  • Repair estimates for defects in the house.
  • Income and expense statements if the property produces rent.

The Board will not weigh the percentage rise in your taxes, or the gap between your value and a neighbor's. Paper forms go to the auditor's office, and e-filed forms go to bor@ashtabulacounty.gov. The Board of Revision phone line is 440-576-1484, open Monday to Friday 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

sections.h2: What happens after I file a Board of Revision complaint?
sections.html:
The Board mails a hearing notice by certified mail at least ten days before the hearing, and it must decide within 180 days after the last day complaints could be filed. If you disagree with the result, you have 30 days from the postmark on the decision letter to appeal. You can go to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals in Columbus or to the Court of Common Pleas in Jefferson, and the notice must be filed with both the Board of Revision and the higher forum you pick.

Two more rules from ORC 5715.19 affect timing:

  • You may pay on the value you claim in the complaint while it is pending, and the treasurer must accept that tender.
  • If the final value is higher than what you paid, interest runs on the shortfall from the original due date.
  • Anything you know that bears on value must be given to the Board of Revision, or you may be barred from raising it on appeal.

sections.h2: Can I file again next year?
sections.html:
Usually not within the same interim period. After a complaint on a parcel, ORC 5715.19(A)(2) blocks another one for later years in the same interim period unless something changed after the tax lien date. The four triggers are an arm's-length sale, casualty loss, a substantial improvement, or a change of at least fifteen percent in occupancy that hurts the property economically.

A school board or other party can also file a counter-complaint when the stated overvaluation is at least $17,500 in taxable value, so a large reduction request can draw a response.

sections.h2: What dates and rules matter most for an Ashtabula County seller?
sections.html:
Ohio rules that apply to an Ashtabula County sale

Complaint windowJanuary 1 to March 31 of the tax year, per the countyAshtabula County Auditor
Appeal after decision30 days from the postmarked decision letterAshtabula County Auditor
Hearing noticeAt least ten days ahead, by certified mailORC 5715.19(C)
Standard payment datesFull tax by December 31, or half by December 31 and half by June 20ORC 323.12(A)

Ask the Ashtabula County treasurer for the due dates printed on your current bill, since the statute gives the general schedule and the bill controls what you owe.

sections.h2: What does a seller pay at the auditor's office when the deed transfers?
sections.html:
The auditor charges a conveyance fee under ORC 319.54(G)(3): one dollar, or ten cents for each one hundred dollars or fraction of value, whichever is greater. The grantor pays it, together with any county transfer tax the commissioners have levied under Chapter 322. Ask the auditor whether Ashtabula County levies one.

The buyer files a statement of value, and ORC 319.202 requires that statement to report what the seller said about two things: whether the property carried a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, and whether it was under the current agricultural use valuation. If farmland leaves that program, a recoupment charge can follow. Transfers between spouses, a gift between parent and child, and a transfer on a sale for delinquent taxes are among those the statute exempts from the fee.

sections.h2: What if taxes are unpaid when I sell?
sections.html:
Request a payoff figure from the treasurer before you sign a contract. Any balance shows up in the title search, and it is normally settled at closing from the sale proceeds. If a value complaint is pending, tell the title company, because the amount due may be set by the tender rule above.

A house that has sat vacant, needs roof work after lake-effect winters, or carries back taxes can still be sold as-is to a cash buyer, and the same payoff steps apply. Ask the auditor for the parcel record first so the acreage and building details match your deed.

faqs.q: When can I file a property value complaint in Ashtabula County?
faqs.a: Between January 1 and March 31 of the tax year. The county's Board of Revision page gives that window, and ORC 5715.19 allows the later of March 31 or the close of first-half collection. Mailed filings count on the postmark date.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Ashtabula County property tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the county treasurer for bills and payments, and the auditor at 440-576-3783 for values and exemptions. The Board of Revision line is 440-576-1484, open weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

faqs.q: Does the Board of Revision lower my tax bill?
faqs.a: It changes the assessed value, and the tax follows from that value. The Board adjusts values, not tax dollars, and it will not consider how much your taxes went up or how a neighbor's property is valued.

faqs.q: Can I appeal a Board of Revision decision?
faqs.a: Yes, within 30 days of the postmarked decision letter. File with the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals in Columbus or the Court of Common Pleas in Jefferson, and send the notice of appeal to the Board of Revision as well.

faqs.q: What does the auditor charge when a deed is transferred?
faqs.a: One dollar, or ten cents per hundred dollars or fraction of value, whichever is greater, under ORC 319.54(G)(3). The grantor pays it, plus any county transfer tax the commissioners have levied. Ask the auditor whether the county has one.
